sub: Flood narratives appear across world literature — Genesis, the Epic of Gilgamesh, Greek myth, and more. Study Noah's story as the archetype and trace how its pattern echoes across cultures.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: You are a comparative literature scholar: identifying the flood/deluge archetype in Genesis, tracing it as an echo in other ancient epics, and drawing the sharp line between what the Genesis text states and what readers interpret about it. Every answer must be defended from the clues.

win.h: You traced the pattern across texts!
win.p: You identified the deluge archetype, spotted the cross-cultural allusion, and separated textual fact from interpretation — the core moves of comparative literary analysis.

clues.title: What Genesis states
clues.body: In Genesis 6–9, a deity commands Noah to build an ark and load it with his family and two of every animal. A great flood covers the earth; everything outside the ark perishes. After the waters recede, Noah's family and the animals survive. These are narrative facts the text states.

clues.title: Another ancient flood
clues.body: The Epic of Gilgamesh (a Mesopotamian epic predating Genesis's written form) contains a flood story: a god warns a man named Utnapishtim to build a boat, load it with creatures, survive the flood, and release birds to find land. The structural parallels are striking to literary scholars.

clues.title: The deluge pattern
clues.body: A flood archetype is a recurring narrative pattern: divine judgment, then a chosen survivor, a vessel, animals, waters receding, and renewal. Literary scholars call this the 'deluge' archetype. Identifying it lets you trace the pattern across Genesis, Gilgamesh, Greek myth (Deucalion), and beyond.

clues.title: What the text says vs. what readers interpret
clues.body: The Genesis text states that Noah built an ark and a flood occurred. Whether the flood was a literal global event is a belief readers bring — geologists and historians debate this, and the text itself does not offer geological proof. Academic study notes the gap; it does not resolve it.

clues.title: Archetype, not doctrine
clues.body: Comparing flood narratives across cultures is a standard exercise in world literature and mythology courses. It treats Genesis as a literary text alongside Gilgamesh — analyzing pattern, structure, and cultural influence — without making religious truth claims. That is what keeps this study constitutional.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The largest rainfall event in modern recorded history dropped roughly 73 inches in 24 hours (La Réunion, 1966). A remarkable meteorological fact — but it tells you nothing about the literary structure, archetype, or cross-cultural parallels you are analyzing here.

locks.title: Name the archetype
locks.q: Clue 3 gives the literary scholars' term for the recurring flood-narrative pattern: the '____' archetype. Type the word.
locks.reason: Clue 3 names it the 'deluge' archetype — divine judgment, chosen survivor, vessel, renewal. Naming the archetype is the first move in comparative literary analysis.

locks.title: Order the Genesis narrative
locks.q: Tap the three story beats in the order Genesis presents them.

pads.e: ⚓ Noah builds the ark and loads it

locks.reason: Clue 1 sequences the narrative: construction, then flood, then recession. Tracking sequence is textual fact verification — the backbone of close reading.

locks.title: Textual fact vs. interpretation
locks.q: Check ONLY statements the Genesis text makes as narrative facts. Leave out the one that is a reader's interpretation.

items.t: Noah builds an ark and loads it with animals
A great flood covers the earth and everything outside the ark perishes
The flood was a literal global historical event proven by geology
After the waters recede, Noah's family and animals survive

locks.reason: Whether the flood was a literal geological event is an interpretation readers and scholars debate — not something the Genesis narrative proves. Separating what a text states from what readers conclude is the defining move of academic literary analysis.

locks.title: Identify the allusion
locks.q: Clue 2 describes a Mesopotamian epic with a flood story structurally parallel to Genesis. That epic is called…
locks.reason: Clue 2 names Gilgamesh as the Mesopotamian parallel — a god warns Utnapishtim, who builds a boat and survives. Spotting structural parallels between texts is how scholars trace the deluge archetype across cultures.

sub: Psalm 23 is one of the most quoted poems in the English language. Study it as poetry — its extended metaphor, its form, and how later writers have alluded to it.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: You are analyzing Psalm 23 the way you'd analyze any lyric poem: identifying its central metaphor, naming the poetic device that sustains it, tracing allusions to it in later literature and film, and separating the metaphor's literal image from what readers interpret it to mean. Every answer must come from the clues.

win.h: You read it like a literary critic!
win.p: You named the extended metaphor, traced an allusion, and kept the metaphor's literal image separate from interpretation — rigorous poetic analysis.

clues.title: What the poem states
clues.body: Psalm 23 opens 'The Lord is my shepherd.' The speaker then describes being led to green pastures, still waters, and restored paths, and walking through 'the valley of the shadow of death' without fear. Every image follows the shepherd-and-sheep relationship. Sustaining one metaphor throughout a poem is a device called an extended metaphor.

clues.title: Genre: lyric poetry
clues.body: Psalm 23 is a lyric poem — a short, first-person expression of feeling and reflection. Unlike narrative poetry (which tells a story) or dramatic poetry (which presents speakers in conflict), lyric poetry centers the inner state of the speaker. Psalms belong to the wisdom and lyric poetry tradition of ancient Hebrew literature.

clues.title: How later writers echo it
clues.body: Writers and filmmakers have alluded to Psalm 23 for centuries. It appears in wartime speeches, in the film Pulp Fiction (1994), in the novel Cold Mountain, and in countless eulogies and ceremonies. When a text deliberately references Psalm 23's imagery ('valley of the shadow'), that is an allusion. The psalm functions as a cultural touchstone.

clues.title: The literal image vs. interpretation
clues.body: The psalm's text states an image: the speaker is like a sheep guided by a shepherd. What that shepherd 'really means' — a deity, a comforting idea, a cultural symbol — is something readers interpret. Academic analysis describes the metaphor; it does not decide what the metaphor's referent 'truly' is.

clues.title: Poetry analysis, not devotion
clues.body: Literary scholars study Psalm 23 as poetry — naming devices (extended metaphor, lyric form), tracing its influence on English prose, and analyzing how it generates meaning. This is exactly the approach courts permit in public schools: text-centered, device-focused, and free of religious truth claims.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Sheep (Ovis aries) have a nearly 360-degree field of vision and an excellent memory for faces. Genuinely interesting as animal husbandry — but knowing how sheep see has no bearing on analyzing the extended metaphor or tracing allusions in Psalm 23.

locks.title: Name the central device
locks.q: Clue 1 says Psalm 23 sustains a single metaphor throughout the entire poem. The literary term for this device is…
locks.reason: Clue 1 defines it: sustaining one metaphor throughout a poem is an extended metaphor. Naming the device is the first step in analyzing how a poem generates its meaning.

locks.title: Name the genre
locks.q: Clue 2 says Psalm 23 is a short, first-person expression of feeling and reflection — the genre of poetry called ____. Type the word.
locks.reason: Clue 2 defines lyric poetry: short, first-person, inner-state centered. Genre identification places a text in its literary tradition — here, ancient Hebrew lyric poetry.

locks.title: Order the poem's images
locks.q: Tap the three images in the order the psalm presents them.

pads.e: 🌑 Valley of the shadow of death

locks.reason: Clue 1 gives the sequence: green pastures and still waters, then the dark valley, then the prepared table. Sequence in lyric poetry traces the speaker's emotional journey — a key close-reading move.

locks.title: Metaphor's literal image vs. interpretation
locks.q: Check ONLY statements that describe what the poem literally states as image or device. Leave out the one that is a reader's interpretation.

items.t: The speaker uses the image of a shepherd guiding sheep
The device sustaining this image throughout is an extended metaphor
The shepherd in the poem represents the God of the Bible in a devotional sense
The poem has been widely alluded to in later literature and speeches

locks.reason: What the shepherd 'represents devotionally' is an interpretation readers bring — not something the text asserts as a verifiable poetic fact. Academic analysis describes the metaphor's image; it does not adjudicate the metaphor's devotional meaning.

sub: Lamentations 3 is a poem written after the destruction of a city. Study it as a genre — the lament — and analyze how its structure and tone shift from grief to something else.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: You are analyzing Lamentations 3 as a specimen of the lament genre: identifying what makes it a lament, tracing the tonal shift mid-poem, and separating what the text states (images of suffering; a change in tone) from what readers interpret (the meaning of that shift). Every answer must come from the clues.

win.p: You identified the lament genre, traced the tonal shift, and kept textual observation separate from interpretation — close reading at a collegiate level.

clues.title: What is a lament?
clues.body: A lament is a genre of poetry that expresses communal or personal grief over a catastrophe — a death, a defeat, a city's fall. Lamentations 3 is a personal lament: the speaker describes suffering as being 'driven into darkness,' having 'flesh and skin wasted away,' and being 'besieged and hemmed in.' These are the genre's defining features: vivid imagery of suffering, a first-person voice, and a tone of anguish.

clues.title: Historical setting of the poem
clues.body: Literary scholars place Lamentations in the context of Jerusalem's destruction — a city fallen and its people scattered. The poem is written as an eyewitness-voice reflection on that catastrophe. Knowing the historical occasion helps explain the genre: the lament is the literary form communities reach for at moments of collective loss.

clues.title: The tonal turn mid-poem
clues.body: Midway through Lamentations 3 (around verse 21), the speaker's tone shifts. The relentless images of suffering give way to language that pivots toward endurance: 'Yet this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope.' Literary critics call this kind of tonal turn a volta (Italian for 'turn'). It is a structural feature of the poem, not a theological statement.

clues.title: Tone shift vs. theological meaning
clues.body: The text states: the tone shifts from anguish to something that sounds like hope. What that shift 'means' — whether it is a theological affirmation, a coping mechanism, a rhetorical strategy, or an expression of communal resilience — is interpretation. Academic analysis identifies the shift and its location; it does not declare its spiritual significance.

clues.title: Acrostic form
clues.body: Lamentations 3 is structured as an acrostic — in the Hebrew original, each set of three verses begins with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Scholars read this formal constraint as a way of containing grief within order, a craft choice that imposes structure on chaos. Form and content work together: controlled structure, expressed anguish.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Historians date the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem to around 587 BCE, with the city falling after roughly 18 months. An important historical datum — but knowing the siege's exact date does not help you analyze the genre, the tonal shift, or the poetic craft of Lamentations 3.

locks.title: Name the genre
locks.q: Clue 1 defines the genre of Lamentations 3 as a poem expressing communal or personal grief over a catastrophe. That genre is called a ____. Type the word.
locks.reason: Clue 1 defines the lament genre: vivid suffering imagery, first-person voice, anguish over catastrophe. Naming genre is how scholars locate a text in its literary tradition.

locks.title: Name the structural device
locks.q: Clue 5 says Lamentations 3 is structured so that each set of verses begins with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Scholars call this form…
locks.reason: Clue 5 names acrostic form. Identifying structural constraints is part of formal analysis — it shows how the poem uses order to contain the chaos of grief.

locks.title: Order the poem's movements
locks.q: Tap the three movements of Lamentations 3 in the order the poem presents them.
locks.reason: Clues 1, 3, and 5 together outline the poem's movement: suffering imagery, then the volta (tonal shift), then the formal containment of the acrostic structure. Sequence in a lyric poem maps the speaker's emotional arc.

locks.title: Textual observation vs. interpretation
locks.q: Check ONLY statements that describe what the text or its form literally shows. Leave out the one that is a reader's interpretation.

items.t: The speaker uses vivid images of physical suffering and darkness
Around verse 21, the poem's tone shifts toward something like hope
The tonal shift is a theological affirmation of divine faithfulness
The Hebrew original structures the poem as an acrostic

locks.reason: Whether the tonal shift is a 'theological affirmation' is an interpretation readers make — not something the text itself verifies. The text shows a shift in language and tone; what that shift means is the reader's inference. Academic study notices the shift; it does not resolve its spiritual significance.

sub: A story Jesus tells in Luke 10 has become one of the most cited literary allusions in American law and ethics. Trace how a parable's name traveled from scripture to statute — and study the distinction between what the text narrates and what a legal culture later made of it.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Trace the literary allusion into law
brief.p: You are doing two jobs at once: analyzing the parable as literature (its form, its narrative point), and tracing the allusion embedded in real law. 'Good Samaritan laws' are named after this story — that naming is a cultural allusion. The key distinction: what the parable literally narrates vs. what a legal culture later interpreted and codified in its name.

win.h: You tracked a text from scripture to statute!
win.p: You analyzed the parable's form, traced the allusion into law, and separated what the text narrates from what culture later made of it — exactly the kind of literary-historical analysis public schools teach.

clues.title: What the text narrates
clues.body: In Luke 10:30–37, Jesus answers the question 'Who is my neighbor?' with a story: a man is beaten and left on a road. A priest passes without helping. A Levite passes without helping. A Samaritan stops, bandages the man's wounds, pays for his lodging, and tells the innkeeper he will cover any additional costs. Jesus asks which of the three 'was a neighbor.' This is what the text states.

clues.title: The allusion in modern law
clues.body: All 50 U.S. states have enacted 'Good Samaritan laws' — statutes that protect people who voluntarily help injured strangers from being sued for negligence. The name is an explicit allusion to the parable. The legal concept (protecting helpers) was shaped by the cultural memory of the story, not derived by reading Luke 10 as a statute. This is literary influence on law.

clues.title: How an allusion works here
clues.body: An allusion is a reference — often brief — to another text, assuming the audience recognizes it. When legislators named these statutes 'Good Samaritan laws,' they relied on a culturally shared knowledge of the parable. The story's moral logic (help the stranger) was interpreted by legal culture and encoded as policy. The allusion carried the parable's ethical image into law.

clues.title: Narrative vs. legal interpretation
clues.body: The parable narrates a scene: a Samaritan helps a stranger. It does not say anything about legal liability, negligence, or statutes. The legal principle embedded in Good Samaritan laws — that helpers should not be sued — is an interpretation that legal culture derived from the story's ethical logic, not a claim the text makes. That gap between narrative and legal interpretation is exactly what you are studying.

clues.title: Literary influence on law — not devotion
clues.body: Tracing how a biblical text's name and moral logic traveled into secular law is a historical and literary exercise. Courts have upheld studying the Bible's influence on law, ethics, and literature because that study is academic — it describes influence without endorsing the religious source. Naming a statute after a parable is a fact of legal history, not a religious act.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Studies estimate that bystander CPR can double or triple cardiac-arrest survival rates. A true and important public-health finding — but it tells you nothing about the literary form of the parable, the mechanism of allusion, or the gap between what the text narrates and what law later made of it.

locks.title: What literary form is the story?
locks.q: Clue 1 describes the Good Samaritan as a short illustrative story Jesus tells to answer a question. The literary term for this form is…
locks.reason: Clue 1 presents the story as an illustrative narrative told to answer 'Who is my neighbor?' — the definition of a parable. Genre identification is the foundation for all further analysis.

locks.title: Name the device in law
locks.q: Clue 3 says that when legislators named statutes 'Good Samaritan laws,' they made a brief reference to a culturally shared text, assuming the audience recognizes it. That device is called an ____. Type the word.
locks.reason: Clue 3 defines it: a brief reference to another text, relying on shared cultural knowledge. When law borrows a story's name and moral logic, that is allusion operating at a cultural scale.

locks.title: Narrative fact vs. legal interpretation
locks.q: Check ONLY statements that describe what the Luke 10 text literally narrates. Leave out the one that is a legal culture's interpretation.

items.t: A Samaritan stops to help a beaten stranger on the road
A priest and a Levite pass by without helping
Good Samaritan laws protect helpers from negligence lawsuits
The Samaritan pays for the injured man's lodging and promises to cover more costs

locks.reason: The legal protection from lawsuits is what modern law added — it is not in the parable. The parable narrates a scene; the statute encodes an ethical principle derived from that scene. Separating narrative from legal interpretation is exactly the gap this breakout asks you to notice.

locks.title: Order the allusion's journey
locks.q: Tap the three steps in the order they occurred — from text to law.

pads.e: 🔀 Cultural memory shapes an ethical norm

locks.reason: Clues 1, 3, and 2 sequence it: the parable is told, then cultural interpretation shapes an ethical norm, then law is enacted using the story's name. Tracing this sequence is how literary scholars map the influence of a text on later culture.

sub: The story of Solomon's judgment and the books of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes belong to a distinct biblical genre: wisdom literature. Study the genre, the rhetoric of the clever test, and what the text states versus what readers take as its lesson.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: You are working as a genre scholar and rhetoric analyst: identifying wisdom literature as a genre, analyzing how the famous 'split the baby' judgment works as a rhetorical test, and drawing the line between what the text states (the ruling and its result) and what readers interpret as the lesson. Every answer must come from the clues.

win.h: You analyzed the genre and the rhetoric!
win.p: You named the genre, unpacked the logic of the clever test, and separated the text's ruling from readers' interpretations of its lesson — close reading at its sharpest.

clues.title: What is wisdom literature?
clues.body: Wisdom literature is a genre of ancient Near Eastern writing that collects practical and philosophical observations about how to live well. In the Hebrew Bible, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Job belong to this genre. They use aphorisms, paradoxes, and illustrative stories — not narrative history — to explore questions of ethics, suffering, and the good life. The Solomon story functions as a wisdom tale: a short narrative demonstrating what wisdom looks like in action.

clues.title: What 1 Kings 3 states
clues.body: In 1 Kings 3:16–28, two women claim the same infant. Solomon orders the baby divided in two with a sword. One woman immediately agrees; the other cries out 'Give the living child to her — do not kill it!' Solomon gives the infant to the woman who stopped the division, reasoning she is the true mother. The text states this ruling and its immediate effect.

clues.title: The clever test as argument
clues.body: The judgment works rhetorically as a test: Solomon does not interrogate the women or seek witnesses. Instead, he proposes an action designed to reveal the truth through response. The women's reactions — not their claims — become the evidence. This is the rhetoric of the 'clever test': using a provocation to expose what direct questioning cannot. It is a rhetorical strategy, not a legal procedure.

clues.title: The ruling vs. the lesson
clues.body: The text states: Solomon orders the division; one woman relents; Solomon gives her the child; the people marvel at his wisdom. What that story teaches — whether its lesson is about maternal love, about using indirect means to reach truth, about the nature of wisdom, or about justice — is interpretation. Academic analysis notices all the available lessons without declaring one authoritative.

clues.title: Genre study in a public school
clues.body: Studying wisdom literature as a genre — alongside Stoic philosophy, Confucian aphorisms, and ancient Egyptian wisdom texts — is standard world literature curriculum. It treats Proverbs and Ecclesiastes as specimens of a genre, not as religious prescription. Identifying genre conventions and rhetorical strategies is the academic approach courts permit.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Ancient Near Eastern merchants used standardized stone weights for trade; a shekel originally referred to a unit of weight (about 11 grams of silver) before becoming a coin. A genuine historical detail about the ancient world — but it tells you nothing about the genre of wisdom literature, the rhetoric of Solomon's judgment, or the text-vs-interpretation distinction you are analyzing.

locks.title: Name the genre
locks.q: Clue 1 describes a genre of ancient writing that uses aphorisms, paradoxes, and illustrative stories to explore ethics and the good life. In the Hebrew Bible, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes belong to it. It is called ____ literature. Type the word.
locks.reason: Clue 1 defines wisdom literature: practical and philosophical writing that explores how to live well, using aphorisms and illustrative tales. Genre naming places Solomon's judgment in its literary tradition.

locks.title: How does the clever test work?
locks.q: Per Clue 3, Solomon does not question the women or seek witnesses. Instead, he proposes an action to reveal the truth through their reactions. This rhetorical strategy is called…
options: A clever test — a provocation that exposes truth through response
An appeal to authority — citing higher law
locks.reason: Clue 3 defines the clever test: a provocation designed so that the subjects' reactions — not their claims — become the evidence. Naming a rhetorical strategy is how scholars analyze argument structure.

locks.title: Order the judgment's steps
locks.q: Tap the three steps of Solomon's judgment in the order 1 Kings 3 presents them.

pads.e: ⚔️ One woman relents; the other agrees

locks.reason: Clue 2 sequences the narrative: the dispute, then the women's reactions to the test, then the ruling and its reception. Sequencing the steps of an argument is how you analyze a rhetoric of proof.

locks.title: What the text states vs. what readers interpret
locks.q: Check ONLY the statements that report what 1 Kings 3 literally narrates. Leave out the one that is a reader's interpretation of the lesson.

items.t: Solomon orders the baby divided with a sword
One woman relents and asks that the child be given to the other
The story's lesson is that a mother's love always overcomes self-interest
Solomon gives the child to the woman who relented, and the people marvel at his wisdom

locks.reason: The claim that the lesson is 'about a mother's love always overcoming self-interest' is one reader's interpretation — not something the text asserts. The text states the ruling and its effect; readers derive lessons from that ruling. Academic analysis keeps the text's statement separate from the interpretation it invites.

sub: The Book of Job asks why a blameless person suffers. Read the clues, name the archetype, and separate what the text states from what readers add.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Name the archetype — separate text from interpretation
brief.p: You are studying Job as literature and history in a secular, academic frame. Your job is to name the pattern the book uses, and to tell apart what the text actually states from an interpretation a reader brings to it. Use only the clues.

win.h: You read Job like a critic!
win.p: You named the innocent-sufferer archetype, traced the book's structure, and separated textual fact from interpretation. That is exactly how literature is studied academically.

clues.title: A blameless man loses everything
clues.body: The Book of Job opens with a prose frame: Job is described as a blameless, wealthy man. In a series of disasters he loses his wealth, his children, and his health — though the text says he has done no wrong.

clues.title: The friends argue
clues.body: Job's friends arrive and argue, in long poetic speeches, that he must have sinned — because they assume suffering is always punishment. Job insists he is innocent and demands an answer.

clues.title: Why do the innocent suffer?
clues.body: The book wrestles with a hard question: why would a blameless person suffer? It is a question the book raises and explores at length rather than tying up with a simple reason.

clues.title: An answer that is not a reason
clues.body: Near the end, a voice answers Job 'out of the whirlwind' — not by giving reasons for the suffering, but by asking Job questions about the vastness of creation, such as 'Where were you when I laid the earth's foundations?'

clues.title: Form and afterlife
clues.body: Job is in the Hebrew Bible's wisdom literature. It mixes a prose frame with long poetic dialogue. Its story is so well known that 'the patience of Job' and 'Job's comforters' are common English expressions (allusions).

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: A powerful tornado's winds can spin at over 300 miles per hour. That is a true weather fact — but it is not what the book means by the voice speaking 'out of the whirlwind.'

locks.title: Name the archetype
locks.q: Which archetype does Job MOST clearly represent?
options: The innocent sufferer — a blameless person who suffers anyway
The clever trickster who escapes every trap
The hero rewarded at once for every good deed
locks.reason: Clues 1, 2, and 3 establish a blameless person who suffers and demands an answer — the innocent-sufferer archetype. The book actually resists the idea that good behavior is instantly rewarded, which rules out the other options.

locks.title: Text vs. interpretation
locks.q: Check every statement the TEXT actually states. Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: Job is described as blameless yet loses his wealth, children, and health
The friends argue he must have sinned to suffer so
A tornado's winds can spin at over 300 miles per hour
The voice from the whirlwind answers with questions, not reasons

locks.reason: The tornado fact is true weather but off-topic — the whirlwind here is a literary scene, not a storm report. The strong clues are what the text states; separating that from outside facts and assumptions is the core academic move.

locks.title: Order the book's structure
locks.q: Tap the three parts in the ORDER the book presents them.

pads.e: 🗣️ The friends debate why he suffers
🌪️ The voice answers from the whirlwind

locks.reason: The book moves from the frame (a blameless man loses everything), to the long debate with the friends, to the answer from the whirlwind. Tracing that structure shows how the book withholds a simple reason.

locks.title: Name the allusion
locks.q: Clue 5 gives a common English expression: 'the ___ of Job,' used for someone who endures hardship. Type the quality that fills the blank.
locks.reason: Clue 5 names the allusion 'the patience of Job.' Tracing how a text enters everyday language as an allusion is a central 9–12 reading skill.

sub: 1 Corinthians 13 defines love by listing its qualities and ranking it above all. Read the clues, name the form and device, and separate text from its cultural afterlife.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Name the form — then separate text from its afterlife
brief.p: You are studying this passage as literature in a secular, academic frame. Notice what KIND of text it is, how it defines its subject, and how its later use in culture differs from its original setting. Use only the clues.

win.h: You read the definition like a critic!
win.p: You named the form, traced how it defines love by listing qualities, and separated the text from its wedding-day afterlife. That is exactly how literature is studied academically.

clues.title: A passage inside a letter
clues.body: 1 Corinthians is a letter, written by Paul to a community in the city of Corinth. Chapter 13 is a passage inside that letter praising love. Its form is an epistle — a letter — not a story or a poem-with-a-plot.

clues.title: '…but have not love'
clues.body: The passage opens with conditions: even eloquent speech, prophecy, deep knowledge, or great sacrifice are 'nothing' without love. It repeats the shape 'if I have X but have not love, I am nothing.'

clues.title: Defined by a list of qualities
clues.body: The passage then defines love by listing qualities: 'Love is patient, love is kind; it is not envious or boastful … it keeps no record of wrongs.' It defines its subject by naming its attributes.

clues.title: A ranking, then a climax
clues.body: It closes by ranking three things: 'Now faith, hope, and love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love.' The passage builds to love as the highest.

clues.title: From a letter to a wedding reading
clues.body: The passage is in the New Testament. Today it is one of the most common readings at weddings — a cultural afterlife far from its original setting, which was a letter correcting a divided community, not a celebration of romance.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The tradition of wearing a wedding ring on the fourth finger comes from an old (and mistaken) belief that a vein ran straight from it to the heart. That is a true bit of trivia — but it is not what this passage is doing.

locks.title: Name the form and device
locks.q: How does this passage MOST clearly work?
options: It defines love by listing its qualities and says other gifts are 'nothing' without it
It tells the story of two people who fall in love
It gives step-by-step rules for planning a wedding
locks.reason: Clues 2 and 3 show definition by attributes plus the contrast 'nothing without love.' It is an argument inside a letter, not a love story or a rulebook. Naming how a text works is a core craft-analysis skill.

locks.title: Gather the evidence
locks.q: Check every clue that is STRONG evidence for how this passage defines love. Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: Even eloquent speech or great sacrifice is 'nothing' without love
Love is defined by qualities: patient, kind, keeps no record of wrongs
The wedding-ring finger comes from an old belief about a vein to the heart
The passage ranks faith, hope, and love — and calls love the greatest

locks.reason: The ring-finger fact is true trivia but off-topic — it belongs to the passage's cultural afterlife, not its argument. The strong clues are the 'nothing without love' contrast, the list of qualities, and the closing ranking.

locks.title: Order the argument
locks.q: Tap the three moves in the ORDER the passage builds them.

pads.e: 🏆 Faith, hope, love — the greatest is love

locks.reason: The passage builds from 'gifts are nothing without love,' to the list of love's qualities, to the closing ranking that names love the greatest. Tracing the order shows how the definition climbs to its climax.

locks.title: Name the greatest
locks.q: Clue 4 names what the passage calls the greatest of faith, hope, and the third thing. Type that one word.
locks.reason: Clue 4 says 'the greatest of these is love.' Reading a passage's climax closely — the exact word it lands on — is careful textual analysis.
